715.title: Mara comes
715.hook: Mara with his bow of flowers and his army of horrors (Buddhacarita 13)
715.howItsDone: Mara's attack on the seated Buddha is painted and carved in Buddhist art, and some Buddhist teachers speak of Mara as a name for whatever in the mind pulls a person away from awakening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nandabala's milk, and your line: strength returns. Did you let someone's help actually help? Today, strong again, he sits beneath a tree, and someone notices. Day seven hundred fifteen.

Flowers on the bow. Flowers on the arrows. The figure who comes for the prince doesn't look like a monster at first. He looks like desire itself, and that's who he is. The prince has eaten, bathed, and walked to a great tree, and he has sat down beneath it, resolved not to get up until he has found what he's looking for. The poem says the whole world grew glad at that. Except one. In his own realm, Mara trembles.
screen: `FLOWERS ON THE BOW.` → `HE SITS, RESOLVED.` → `ONLY MARA TREMBLES.`

segments.voice: First, who Mara is. The poem introduces him with two names at once. In the world, it says, he is called the god of love, the one with the flowered bow. And he is also Mara, the enemy of freedom. Ashvaghosha joins them on purpose. The one who makes us want and the one who keeps us bound are, in this poem, the same figure. Second, his fear. His sons and daughters ask why he's troubled. He tells them: that man under the tree has put on the armor of resolve. If he wins, he'll lead others out of my realm, and it will stand empty. So I'll break his vow before he finishes. Third, the bow. Mara takes his flower bow and goes to the tree with his children. He speaks first. Get up, he says, in paraphrase. You're a warrior by birth. Go back to your duty, rule, make offerings, win heaven the proper way. Give up this begging road. If you won't rise, here's my arrow. And he lets it fly. The poem says the prince doesn't stir. He doesn't even seem to notice it. The arrow Mara trusts does nothing at all. Fourth, the army. Mara is shaken, and he changes weapons. If desire won't work, fear might. He calls up his army, and the poem fills the air around the tree with horrors: creatures with the faces of beasts, many-armed, many-headed, carrying spears, clubs, swords and burning trees, howling. They surround the seated man on every side. That's where the poem leaves him today, and so will we. Notice Mara's order of attack. He tries the flowers first. The soft weapon. The appeal to duty, to sense, to pleasure. Only when the flower arrow fails does he reach for the horrors. The bow of flowers comes before the army.
screen: `THE GOD OF LOVE, THE ENEMY OF FREEDOM.` · `IF HE WINS, MY REALM IS EMPTY.` · `THE FLOWER ARROW DOES NOTHING.` · `AN ARMY OF HORRORS.` · then, large: `THE BOW OF FLOWERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one fear, gently. Settle, and breathe. Let the body be as still as you comfortably can, like someone seated beneath a tree. Now let one fear come forward. Not the biggest. Just one that's around today. A conversation. A bill. A test result. When it arrives, name it quietly, in a few words: this is the fear of being alone. This is the fear of not having enough. Say it the way you'd name a bird you can see. Then let your breath stay slow, and keep sitting. You don't have to fight it. The bell holds the time.
Mara comes. The god of desire and enemy of freedom shoots his flower arrow at the seated prince, and when it fails, calls up an army of horrors. Today's word.
Your line: the bow of flowers. Today, notice when something pulls at you softly, with sweetness instead of force, and give it one breath before you follow. Day seven hundred fifteen.

Mara's arrow wounds the prince

fork.setup: you're seated beneath a tree, resolved not to rise. a figure with a bow of flowers tells you to get up and go back to your duty, and draws an arrow. what do you do?
options: get up and argue with him.
fork.reveal: the prince doesn't stir. the arrow flies and does nothing, so Mara changes weapons and calls up his army of horrors.

original.note: Sanskrit and Pali: the name of the tempter in Buddhist stories, who tries to stop the awakening.

trapdoor: what you thought: Mara is a monster who attacks with an army.
what it means: in the poem he comes first as desire, with a flower bow and a reasonable speech, and only then with horrors.
what a scholar hears: Ashvaghosha identifies Mara with Kama, the god of love, so the enemy of freedom and the lord of desire are one figure.

sources.ref: Buddhacarita 13 (Mara and his family, the flower bow, his speech, the arrow, the army)

716.title: Mara defeated
716.hook: the army scatters; a voice from the sky tells Mara to give up (Buddhacarita 13)
716.howItsDone: Buddhist art shows the Buddha seated at the moment of victory over Mara, and in some traditions the story is retold at festivals of the awakening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mara comes, and your line: the bow of flowers. Did you notice a soft pull and give it a breath? Today the army attacks. Day seven hundred sixteen.

The army doesn't stop to talk. Mara has already tried talking: a speech about duty, a flower arrow, and the man under the tree didn't stir. So now everything the army can lift, it throws. Rocks, trees, spears, fire. The air around the tree fills with howling and smoke. In the middle of it, one man sits with his legs crossed and his eyes steady. He doesn't answer. He doesn't flinch. And then a voice speaks from somewhere above the noise, from someone nobody can see.
screen: `ROCKS, TREES, SPEARS, FIRE.` → `ONE MAN, SITTING STILL.` → `A VOICE FROM ABOVE.`

segments.voice: First, the attack. The poem gives the army full force. Some hurl boulders. Some swing whole trees. Some throw weapons, some breathe fire, some try to terrify him with shrieks and faces. Second, what happens to it. Nothing lands. In the poem, paraphrased here, what's thrown at him stops in the air, or falls short, or turns harmless. The fire doesn't burn him. The noise doesn't move him. Weapons that would break anyone else fail on this one seated man. Third, the voice. Then a being in the sky, unseen, speaks to Mara. Give up this useless effort, it says. Lay down your anger. You can no more shake this man than the wind can shake the great mountain. Fire might lose its heat, water its wetness, the earth its firmness, before he gives up his resolve. He has made his vow, and the time has come for it to be fulfilled. Fourth, the scattering. Mara hears it. He looks at the man under the tree, still unmoved. And the poem says he goes away disheartened, his effort spent, and his army scatters in every direction. The sky clears. Flowers fall from it. Look at how the victory is won. The prince never lifts a hand. He never argues back, never calls for help, never fights. The poem doesn't even give him a line. His whole answer to the army is to keep sitting. And the army, which could break anything that resisted, has nothing to push against. What scatters it isn't a stronger army. It's stillness that won't be moved. Tomorrow the night goes on, and the poem turns from what he refused to what he sees.
screen: `THE ARMY THROWS EVERYTHING.` · `NOTHING LANDS.` · `NO WIND SHAKES THE MOUNTAIN.` · `MARA GOES, DISHEARTENED.` · then, large: `THE ARMY SCATTERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one fear pass. Settle, and breathe. Bring back the fear you named yesterday, or another that's here today. Let it come close. Don't push it away and don't follow it. Just keep sitting, the way the prince keeps sitting while the army howls. Feel the breath come in and go out underneath it. Watch the fear rise, peak, and begin to thin. If it doesn't thin, that's all right. Let it stay, and keep breathing. Fears, like armies, sometimes run out of things to throw. The bell holds the time.
Mara defeated. The army throws everything at the seated prince and nothing lands; a voice from the sky tells Mara to give up, and his army scatters. Today's word.
Your line: the army scatters. Today, when something comes at you loud and fast, try not answering for one breath, and see what's left of it when the noise stops. Day seven hundred sixteen.

fork.setup: you're Mara. your flower arrow failed, and now your whole army has failed too. a voice from the sky tells you to give up. what do you do?
options: sit down beside him and learn.
fork.reveal: Mara looks once more at the unmoved man and goes away disheartened. his army scatters, the sky clears, and flowers fall.

original.note: Sanskrit: unmoving, steady; also a word for a mountain.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha defeated Mara in a battle.
what it means: in the poem he never fights; the army's weapons fail, a voice tells Mara to stop, and Mara leaves.
what a scholar hears: Ashvaghosha gives the victory no speech from the prince at all, so his steadiness is the whole answer, likened to a mountain no wind can move.

sources.ref: Buddhacarita 13 (the army's attack, the voice from the sky, Mara's departure)

717.title: Perfect knowledge
717.hook: the night of awakening, told in verse (Buddhacarita 14)
717.howItsDone: The awakening is remembered at Vesak (or Wesak), when in many places temples are lit and people gather to meditate, keep precepts and hear teachings; in some places devotees sit through the night in memory of the night under the tree.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mara defeated, and your line: the army scatters. Did you let one fear pass without chasing it? Today the field is empty, and the night is still young. Day seven hundred seventeen.

The noise is over. Mara's army, the arrows, the shrieking shapes, the whole storm of the last two lessons, is gone. What's left is a man sitting under a tree, and a night ahead of him. A story could stop here, with the victory. The poem doesn't. It slows down. It walks through the hours of the dark one stretch at a time, the way someone who can't sleep feels every hour of a long night. The battle was loud. The awakening, in Ashvaghosha's telling, is quiet, and it takes all night.
screen: `THE BATTLE IS OVER.` → `A MAN UNDER A TREE.` → `THE NIGHT, HOUR BY HOUR.`

segments.voice: First, he looks back. In the first watch of the night, the poem says, he remembers his own former lives, one after another: where he was born, what his name was, what happened to him. And what he feels, looking back, is not pride. It's compassion, for every being caught in that long turning. Second, he looks out. In the middle watch, the poem gives him a clear, divine sight. He sees beings everywhere dying and being born again, rising and falling according to what they have done. Good deeds, hard deeds, and their fruit. The whole world, the poem says, seems to him to have no solid core, like the stem of a plantain plant, layers with nothing hard in the middle. Third, he looks in. In the last watch, he asks the question under all the others: where do old age and death come from? From birth. And birth? From becoming. Link by link, he follows the chain back, down to not knowing, ignorance. And then he sees it the other way: when ignorance ends, the chain comes apart, link by link, all the way to the end of old age and death. And fourth, the dawn. As the night ends, the poem says, he reaches perfect knowledge. He has become the Buddha, the awakened one. The earth sways, flowers fall, and the gods rejoice. But at the center of all that color is one still figure who has finished a long question. The discourses tell this night in a plainer way, with the same three watches. The poem adds the beauty. Both agree on the shape: looking back, looking out, looking in, and then light.
screen: `FIRST WATCH: HIS OWN PAST LIVES.` · `MIDDLE WATCH: ALL BEINGS, COMING AND GOING.` · `LAST WATCH: THE CHAIN OF CAUSES.` · `DAWN: THE AWAKENED ONE.` · then, large: `THE NIGHT OF KNOWING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit through the evening quietly. Tonight, if you can, give the evening a few unhurried minutes with no screen and no sound. For now, a small version. Settle. For a few breaths, look back over today: what happened, without judging it. Then look out: the people around you, near and far, each going through their own day. Then look in: just this breath, coming and going. Let the order be enough. The bell holds the time.
Perfect knowledge. Through the watches of one night he remembers, sees and understands, and at dawn he is the Buddha. Today's word.
Your line: the night of knowing. Tonight, before sleep, sit for a minute in the dark and let the day settle, back, out and in. Day seven hundred seventeen.

link by link, and then sees the chain come apart when ignorance ends.

fork.setup: you've just faced down an army of fears. it's dark, and you're still under the tree. what do you do?
options: get up and celebrate the victory.
stay seated and keep looking, all night.
go and find your old companions.
fork.reveal: he stays. the poem gives the whole night to remembering, seeing and understanding, and the awakening comes at dawn.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha just suddenly understood everything.
what it means: in the poem, the knowing unfolds watch by watch: past lives, all beings, the chain of causes, then dawn.
what a scholar hears: the discourses tell the same night as three knowings in three watches (MN 36); Ashvaghosha keeps that frame and dresses it in verse.

sources.ref: Buddhacarita 14 (the watches of the night, dependent origination, the awakening at dawn)
Majjhima Nikaya 36 (the three knowledges in the three watches)

718.title: The wheel turned
718.hook: the first sermon and the five companions (Buddhacarita 15)
718.howItsDone: The first teaching is remembered in Buddhist communities; in Theravada lands the full moon of Asalha (Asalha Puja) marks it, and the wheel, the dharma-chakra, appears on temple roofs, gates and flags as a sign of the teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, perfect knowledge, and your line: the night of knowing. Did you give the evening a quiet minute, back, out and in? Today the Buddha stands up and walks toward people. Day seven hundred eighteen.

Five men in a park near Benares see someone walking toward them, and they make a plan. They know him. They practiced hard beside him once, fasting and straining, until he gave it up and started eating again. They decided he'd gone soft. So now, as he comes closer, they agree among themselves: we won't stand up for him. We won't greet him. Let him sit where he likes. Then he arrives. And the plan doesn't survive the moment.
screen: `FIVE OLD COMPANIONS.` → `A PLAN NOT TO STAND.` → `THEN HE ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: First, the welcome they didn't intend. In the poem, as he draws near, the five find themselves rising anyway. The Vinaya's telling adds the details: one takes his bowl and robe, one brings water, one makes ready a seat. Their agreement falls apart in their hands. They still speak to him as an old friend, by name, and he tells them gently not to: he has become something new. Second, the middle way. What he teaches them first is not a list of rules. It's a road between two ditches. On one side, the life of pleasure he left in the palace. On the other, the life of self-punishment these five still believe in, the starving and the straining. Neither one leads to peace, he says. There is a middle path, and it is the one he found. Third, the truths. He names suffering, its arising, its ending, and the path that leads to its ending. And he lays out that path: right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. The poem sets all of this into verse, so the first teaching becomes something you could almost sing. And fourth, the first one who sees. Kaundinya, one of the five, understands. The discourses say that when he did, a cry went up through the heavens: the wheel of the teaching has been set rolling, and no one in the world can turn it back. That's the picture behind today's title. A wheel, once pushed, keeps rolling. The Buddha gave it the first push, in a deer park, to five men who had planned not to stand up.
screen: `THE FIVE RISE ANYWAY.` · `A ROAD BETWEEN TWO DITCHES.` · `THE TRUTHS AND THE PATH.` · `KAUNDINYA SEES IT.` · then, large: `THE WHEEL, IN VERSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say the middle way in one line. Settle, and breathe. Think of one place in your life where you swing between two ditches: too much and too little, all in or all out, coffee or nothing, work all night or not at all. Now try to say the middle of it in one plain line, the way you'd say it to a friend. Not a rule to obey. Just a road between the two. Then let the line go and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The wheel turned. The first teaching, to five old companions in a deer park: the middle way, the truths and the path, and Kaundinya understands. Today's word.
Your line: the wheel, in verse. Today, when you catch yourself swinging to one extreme, say your one line of middle way quietly, and take one step down the middle. Day seven hundred eighteen.

the first teaching says harsh self-punishment is the way to peace
it names self-torment as one of the two ditches, beside a life of pleasure.
Kaundinya was the first of the five to understand
and the discourses say a cry went up that the wheel had been set rolling.

fork.setup: you're one of the five. the man you think gave up is walking toward you. you've all agreed not to stand. what happens?
options: you walk away before he arrives.
fork.reveal: the agreement falls apart as he comes near: they rise, and the Vinaya says they took his bowl, brought water and made ready a seat.

original.note: Sanskrit dharmacakra, the wheel of the teaching (Pali dhammacakka).

trapdoor: what you thought: the first sermon was a list of rules.
what it means: it starts with a middle way between pleasure and self-torment, then the truths and the path.
what a scholar hears: the Pali discourse that tells it is called the turning of the wheel of the dhamma (SN 56.11); the poem retells it in verse.

sources.ref: Buddhacarita 15 (the journey to Benares, the five, the first teaching)
Vinaya, Mahavagga 1.6 (the five rise despite their agreement: bowl, water, seat)

719.title: Many come
719.hook: the fire-worshipers, the kings, the friends (Buddhacarita 16)
719.howItsDone: The Fire Sermon is still chanted and taught in Theravada communities, and in some communities monasteries and temples receive newcomers, from curious visitors to people asking to ordain, with a simple welcome and a place to sit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the wheel turned, and your line: the wheel, in verse. Did you find one line of middle way for your own day? Today the wheel starts picking up people. Day seven hundred nineteen.

A rich young man wakes up in the middle of the night in a beautiful house. The lamps are still burning. The musicians who played for him have fallen asleep where they sat, sprawled and snoring. And he sees it all, suddenly, as ugly and sad. If that sounds familiar, it should. It's the prince's night, a few cantos back, happening to someone else. His name is Yasas. He walks out of the house in distress, and he finds the Buddha. And after him, the poem says, his friends come too.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN WAKES AT NIGHT.` → `THE PRINCE'S NIGHT, AGAIN.` → `HE WALKS OUT, AND FRIENDS FOLLOW.`

segments.voice: Canto sixteen is a canto of arrivals. First, the friends. Yasas comes, and is taught, and goes forth. Then his friends hear what he's done, and they come to see for themselves. The teaching travels the way news often travels: one friend tells another. Second, the fire-worshipers. At Uruvilva lives a famous ascetic of the Kashyapa family, a keeper of sacred fires, with his brothers and a crowd of followers. The Buddha asks to spend the night in the hall where the fire is kept. There's a fierce serpent in there, they warn him. He goes in anyway, and in the morning the serpent lies calm in his bowl. Even so, the story has the eldest brother hold on to his pride for a while, until at last he yields. He and his followers give up their fire rites, and the tradition says they threw their fire gear into the river. Downstream, his brothers see it floating past, and come upriver to find out what happened. Third, the fire sermon. To these fire-keepers the Buddha speaks in their own language: everything is burning. The eye is burning, the ear is burning, the mind is burning, with the fires of desire, anger and delusion. People who tended fire all their lives hear about a fire they can put out. Fourth, the king. In Rajagriha, King Bimbisara, who once offered the young wanderer half a kingdom, hears he has come back. The prince had promised to return once he found what he was looking for. He keeps the promise. The king comes out to listen, and is moved. Friends, fire-keepers, a king. Many come.
screen: `YASAS, THEN HIS FRIENDS.` · `THE KEEPERS OF THE FIRE.` · `EVERYTHING IS BURNING.` · `A KING, AND A PROMISE KEPT.` · then, large: `MANY COME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: welcome someone new. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who is new somewhere you already belong: a new coworker, a new neighbor, a new face in a class, a group chat or a place of worship. Picture the door they walked through, and how it might look from their side. Then decide on one small welcome you could give today: a name remembered, a seat offered, a question asked. Hold that, and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Many come. Yasas and his friends, the Kashyapa brothers with their fire, and King Bimbisara, all arriving in one canto. Today's word.
Your line: many come. Today, when someone new walks in, be the one who says their name and makes room. Day seven hundred nineteen.

what it means: in the poem they come one by one and in groups: a friend, then friends, then a family of fire-keepers, then a king.
what a scholar hears: the Pali Vinaya tells the same run of arrivals, Yasa, the Kassapas and Bimbisara (Mahavagga 1), and the fire sermon is SN 35.28.

Samyutta Nikaya 35.28 (Adittapariyaya Sutta, the fire sermon)

720.title: Mahakassapa comes
720.hook: the great ascetic comes to him (Buddhacarita 17)
720.howItsDone: Mahakassapa is honored in Theravada as a model of forest and ascetic practice, and in Zen lineages as the first heir of the teaching after the Buddha. Monks in forest traditions still keep some of the strict practices he is remembered for.

segments.voice: Yesterday, many come, and your line: many come. Did you make room for someone new? Today one more arrives, a man who had already given up nearly everything. Day seven hundred twenty.

Two robes on a roadside. One is a patched outer robe, but soft, folded into a seat under a tree. The other is rough hemp, worn thin, stitched together from rags. In a little while, the two men wearing them will swap. The man with the soft robe is a seeker who has already left a wealthy home. The man with the rags is the Buddha. This is how the discourses remember the meeting with Kassapa, the one later called Mahakassapa, great Kassapa. And the poem, in its seventeenth canto, sends him walking toward the Buddha too.
screen: `TWO ROBES ON A ROADSIDE.` → `ONE SOFT, ONE RAGGED.` → `KASSAPA IS COMING.`

segments.voice: First, what he left. Tradition remembers Kassapa as born into a wealthy brahmin family, and leaving it all, house, riches, a wife, to go looking for freedom. Later tradition adds a tender detail: his wife, Bhadda, wanted the same thing, and the two of them went forth together, parting at a crossroads to walk different roads. Second, the meeting. In his own words in the discourses, Kassapa says he saw the Buddha sitting by a shrine on the road between Rajagaha and Nalanda, and knew at once: this is my teacher. He bowed and said so. And the Buddha taught him, there by the road. Third, the robes. Kassapa folded his cloak for the Buddha to sit on. The Buddha remarked how soft it was. Kassapa offered it. And the Buddha gave him his own worn rag-robe in return. It's a small, strange exchange, and some readers take it as a sign: the teacher handing his robe to someone who would carry the teaching on. Fourth, what he became. The discourses list Kassapa as foremost among the monks who kept the strict ascetic practices: living in the forest, eating only alms food, wearing rag-robes. He came after the first five, after Yasas and the fire-keepers. He wasn't the first. But in the stories, he became one of the great ones, and tradition says that after the Buddha's death it was Kassapa who called the monks together to remember what had been taught. The great ones don't all arrive at the start.
screen: `A WEALTHY HOME, LEFT BEHIND.` · `THIS IS MY TEACHER.` · `A SOFT CLOAK FOR A RAG-ROBE.` · `FOREMOST IN THE STRICT PRACTICES.` · then, large: `THE GREAT ONES ARRIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor someone who came late. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who joined something after you did: a family, a team, a friendship circle, a community. Maybe they came in quietly, and you've never thought of them as part of the founding story. Notice one thing they carry now that no one else does. If you like, plan to tell them so. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Mahakassapa comes. A wealthy brahmin who left home, met the Buddha by a roadside shrine, and traded his soft cloak for a rag-robe. Today's word.
Your line: the great ones arrive. Today, tell one person who came later than you what they've added. Day seven hundred twenty.

screen: `DAY 720 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE REST OF THE POEM.`

folded as a seat, then given

he came later, after the five, Yasas and the fire-keepers.
the Buddha and Kassapa exchanged robes
Kassapa gave his soft cloak, and the Buddha gave his worn rag-robe.

forest living, alms food and rag-robes.

fork.setup: you're Kassapa. you've folded your good cloak for the teacher to sit on, and he says how soft it is. what do you do?
fork.reveal: Kassapa offers it, and the Buddha gives him his own worn rag-robe in return.

trapdoor: what you thought: the great disciples were all there at the start.
what it means: Kassapa came later, after the first five and the fire-keepers, and still became one of the great ones.
what a scholar hears: in the discourses Kassapa tells the meeting himself, ending with the robe exchange (SN 16.11).

sources.ref: Buddhacarita 17 (the going forth of great disciples, including Kashyapa)
Samyutta Nikaya 16.11 (Civara Sutta: the meeting at the Bahuputta shrine and the exchange of robes)
Anguttara Nikaya 1 (Etadagga Vagga: foremost in the ascetic practices)
Samyutta Nikaya 16.5 (Jinna Sutta: Kassapa as forest dweller, alms-food eater and rag-robe wearer)

721.title: The rest of the poem
721.hook: the full poem survives in Tibetan and Chinese, carrying the story to the relics
721.howItsDone: English translations of the full Buddhacarita follow the Sanskrit where it survives and the Tibetan or Chinese versions after that; the Buddha's relics are honored at stupas across Asia.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mahakassapa comes, and your line: the great ones arrive. Did you thank someone who came later than you? Today, the end of the week, and the end of the poem's road. Day seven hundred twenty-one.

A book with its last chapters torn out, and a friend overseas who happens to own a copy. That's roughly the situation with this poem. The Sanskrit text, the language Ashvaghosha wrote in, breaks off partway through the story. If that were all there was, the life in verse would stop in the middle of the night under the tree, before the dawn. But the poem was carried abroad and translated, into Tibetan and into Chinese. And in those versions, the story keeps going, all the way to the end.
screen: `A BOOK WITH ITS LAST PAGES GONE.` → `THE SANSKRIT BREAKS OFF.` → `TIBETAN AND CHINESE CARRY ON.`

segments.voice: So what's in the rest of the poem? Four stretches. First, the gifts of land. A rich merchant, Anathapindika, buys a prince's grove for the Buddha and the monks, so they have a place to stay through the rains. The teaching has a home. Second, the return. The Buddha goes back to his father's city, the one he left through the silent gates. The king who tried to keep him in meets a son who comes back as a teacher, and listens. Third, the trouble and the welcome. A cousin, Devadatta, turns against him and sets a maddened elephant loose in his path, and the elephant stops and grows calm before him. And a courtesan, Amrapali, welcomes him into her mango grove and gives it to the community. The poem honors her gift. Fourth, the end. The Buddha, old and ill, makes his last journey, lies down between two sala trees at Kushinagara, gives his last teaching, and passes into final nirvana. And near its close the poem goes one step further than the death: the kings of the region quarrel over his relics, nearly go to war, and then agree to share them, each carrying a portion home to honor. So the story closes with the life scattered across many places, and kept. And notice the echo. The poem itself had the same fate. Scattered, carried, kept in other languages. Look back at this week: Mara came with a bow of flowers; Mara was defeated; the night of knowing; the wheel turned; many came; Mahakassapa came. And now the rest of the poem, carried home by other hands.
screen: `A GROVE FOR THE RAINS.` · `HOME TO HIS FATHER'S CITY.` · `AN ELEPHANT, A MANGO GROVE.` · `THE SALA TREES, AND THE RELICS SHARED.` · then, large: `THE POEM TRAVELED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look up where the poem traveled. After the sit, if you're curious, open a map and trace the roads a book could take from northern India, north to Tibet, and by other roads to China. For now, settle and breathe, and let the picture come: a story copied by hand, wrapped, carried on someone's back through cold passes, and read aloud somewhere new. Think of one story in your own life that someone else carried to you. Rest with that. The bell holds the time.
The rest of the poem. Where the Sanskrit breaks off, the Tibetan and Chinese carry the story on, to the last journey and the relics shared. Today's word.
screen: `THE REST OF THE POEM — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the poem traveled. Today, pass one good story on to someone who hasn't heard it, so it travels a little further. Day seven hundred twenty-one.
